description:
Scenario: handle_metadata_changes runs against a default-impl backend (the override case is fine). filter_changes_array at metadata.rs:214-276 builds ids_for_fetch by collecting every id in the response array, then calls backend.get_objects::<Metadata>(caller, account_id, Some(&ids_for_fetch), None) in a single call.

For a healthy default-impl backend, this means a single batch fetch of every changed id. For a database-backed default-impl backend, this is potentially:
(a) An IN-clause with thousands of items, blowing past common DB query argument limits (postgres ~32k, SQLite default 999).
(b) A network round-trip pulling thousands of objects' full payload over the wire — expensive when /changes was supposed to be lightweight.
(c) Memory pressure: lookup HashMap (metadata.rs:245) holds every returned object plus their cloned Metadata representations.

There is no max-batch chunking, no cap, no get_objects size guard. Mail-server's own /changes path (the canonical) is implemented differently — the override pattern exists precisely because the default-impl path is known to be expensive. But that's a workspace concern hidden behind one phrase in the rustdoc ('per-Id re-fetch cost').

Maintenance consequence: a downstream contributor writes the simplest possible default-impl backend (no override of get_metadata_changes), then their first production load hits /changes with a large window and the backend pulls thousands of objects per request. The contributor profiles, sees the get_objects call, doesn't understand why it's the entire change-window worth of data, files an issue.

Fix direction: either:
(i) Add a max-batch cap (configurable via MetadataBackend method or a constant) and chunk get_objects calls.
(ii) Document loudly that the default-impl path is O(window_size) per /changes call, recommend backends override get_metadata_changes for any production deployment.
title: filter_changes_array post-fetches via get_objects with no max-batch guard — pathological 10k-id /changes window triggers single 10k get_objects call
